records.question: Under the enacted statutory text of Section 11 of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (scheduled to commence on 13 May 2027 under G.S.R. 843(E)), what specific information will a Data Principal be entitled to obtain from a Data Fiduciary?
records.proposed_answer: Under the enacted statutory scheme of Section 11(1) of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (which is scheduled to commence on 13 May 2027 pursuant to Notification G.S.R. 843(E) and is not yet in force as of 16 October 2026), a Data Principal who has previously given consent will have the right to obtain from the Data Fiduciary upon request: (a) a summary of personal data which is being processed by such Data Fiduciary and the processing activities undertaken with respect to such personal data; (b) the identities of all other Data Fiduciaries and Data Processors with whom the personal data has been shared, along with a description of the personal data so shared; and (c) any other information related to the personal data and its processing as may be prescribed.
statutory_citations: Section 11, Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023

evidence_passages.verbatim_text:
11. Right to access information about personal data.-(1) The Data Principal shall have the right to obtain from the Data Fiduciary to whom she has previously given consent, including consent as referred to in clause (a) of section 7 (hereinafter referred to as the said Data Fiduciary), for processing of personal data, upon making to it a request in such manner as may be prescribed,-

(a) a summary of personal data which is being processed by such Data Fiduciary and the processing activities undertaken by that Data Fiduciary with respect to such personal data;

(b) the identities of all other Data Fiduciaries and Data Processors with whom the personal data has been shared by such Data Fiduciary, along with a description of the personal data so shared; and

(c) any other information related to the personal data of such Data Principal and its processing, as may be prescribed.

records.question: What statutory duties are established for a Data Fiduciary regarding correction, completion, updating, and erasure under the enacted text of Section 12 of the DPDP Act, 2023 once it comes into force?
records.proposed_answer: Under the enacted text of Section 12 of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (appointed to commence on 13 May 2027 under G.S.R. 843(E) and not yet in force as of 16 October 2026), a Data Principal will possess statutory rights under Section 12(1) to correction, completion, updating, and erasure of personal data. Upon receiving such a request, under Section 12(2) the Data Fiduciary shall: (a) correct inaccurate or misleading personal data; (b) complete incomplete personal data; and (c) update the personal data. Furthermore, under Section 12(3), upon receiving an erasure request, the Data Fiduciary shall erase the personal data unless retention is necessary for the specified purpose or legal compliance.
statutory_citations: Section 12, Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023

evidence_passages.verbatim_text:
12. Right to correction and erasure of personal data.-(1) A Data Principal shall have the right to correction, completion, updating and erasure of her personal data for the processing of which she has previously given consent, including consent as referred to in clause (a) of section 7, in accordance with any requirement or procedure under any law for the time being in force.

(2) A Data Fiduciary shall, upon receiving a request for correction, completion or updating from a Data Principal,-

(a) correct the inaccurate or misleading personal data;

- (b) complete the incomplete personal data; and
- (c) update the personal data.

(3) A Data Principal shall make a request in such manner as may be prescribed to the Data Fiduciary for erasure of her personal data, and upon receipt of such a request, the Data Fiduciary shall erase her personal data unless retention of the same is necessary for the specified purpose or for compliance with any law for the time being in force.

records.question: Under the enacted scheme of Section 13 of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, must a Data Principal exhaust internal grievance redressal mechanisms before approaching the Data Protection Board of India?
records.proposed_answer: Yes. Under the enacted statutory provisions of Section 13 of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (scheduled to commence on 13 May 2027 pursuant to Notification G.S.R. 843(E) and not yet in force as of 16 October 2026), a Data Principal will have readily available means of grievance redressal under Section 13(1). Section 13(3) explicitly dictates that the Data Principal shall exhaust the opportunity of redressing her grievance under Section 13 before approaching the Data Protection Board.
statutory_citations: Section 13, Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023

evidence_passages.verbatim_text:
13. Right of grievance redressal.-(1) A Data Principal shall have the right to have readily available means of grievance redressal provided by a Data Fiduciary or Consent Manager in respect of any act or omission of such Data Fiduciary or Consent Manager regarding the performance of its obligations in relation to the personal data of such Data Principal or the exercise of her rights under the provisions of this Act and the rules made thereunder.

(2) The Data Fiduciary or Consent Manager shall respond to any grievances referred to in sub-section (1) within such period as may be prescribed from the date of its receipt for all or any class of Data Fiduciaries.

(3) The Data Principal shall exhaust the opportunity of redressing her grievance under this section before approaching the Board.

records.question: What statutory obligation will be placed upon a Data Fiduciary to protect personal data by taking security safeguards under the enacted Section 8(5) of the DPDP Act, 2023, and what is its commencement status?
records.proposed_answer: Under the enacted text of Section 8(5) of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (which commences on 13 May 2027 under Notification G.S.R. 843(E) and is uncommenced as of 16 October 2026), a Data Fiduciary is mandated to protect personal data in its possession or under its control, including in respect of any processing undertaken by it or on its behalf by a Data Processor, by taking reasonable security safeguards to prevent personal data breach. (Note: As of October 2026 prior to the 13 May 2027 commencement, data protection security requirements under existing law remain governed under the Information Technology Act, 2000).

records.question: What legal requirements must be fulfilled for consent given by a Data Principal under the enacted provisions of Section 6(1) of the DPDP Act, 2023, and when do they take effect?
records.proposed_answer: Under the enacted text of Section 6(1) of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (scheduled for commencement on 13 May 2027 under Notification G.S.R. 843(E) and not yet in force as of 16 October 2026), consent given by the Data Principal shall be free, specific, informed, unconditional, and unambiguous with a clear affirmative action. It must signify an agreement to the processing of her personal data for the specified purpose and be limited to such personal data as is necessary for such specified purpose.

records.question: Under the enacted provisions of Section 8(6) of the DPDP Act, 2023, who must be notified by the Data Fiduciary in the event of a personal data breach once the section commences?
records.proposed_answer: Under Section 8(6) of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (enacted and appointed to commence on 13 May 2027 under Notification G.S.R. 843(E), hence uncommenced as of 16 October 2026), in the event of a personal data breach, the Data Fiduciary shall give intimation of such breach to both the Data Protection Board of India and each affected Data Principal, in such form and manner as may be prescribed.

records.question: Under the enacted statutory text of Section 33(1) of the DPDP Act, 2023, what prerequisites govern the imposition of monetary penalties by the Board once the penal provisions commence?
records.proposed_answer: Under the enacted provisions of Section 33(1) of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (scheduled to commence on 13 May 2027 under G.S.R. 843(E) and uncommenced as of 16 October 2026), if the Board determines on conclusion of an inquiry that breach of the provisions of the Act or rules by a person is significant, it may, after giving the person an opportunity of being heard, impose such monetary penalty specified in the Schedule.

records.question: What is the operational status of Section 43A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 as of 16 October 2026, and on what exact date does its omission under Section 44(2) of the DPDP Act, 2023 take legal effect?
records.proposed_answer: As of 16 October 2026, Section 43A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 remains operative law and legally enforceable. While Section 44(2)(a) of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 provides for the omission of Section 43A, Notification G.S.R. 843(E) (published 13 November 2025) specifies that Section 44(2) commences on the expiry of eighteen months from publication. Computing eighteen calendar months from 13 November 2025 under Section 9 of the General Clauses Act, 1897 establishes that Section 44(2) commences on 13 May 2027. Therefore, prior to 13 May 2027, Section 43A IT Act remains in force.

records.question: Under current law, how does Section 61 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 establish the admissibility of an electronic record as defined under Section 2(1)(t) of the Information Technology Act, 2000, and what statutory proviso applies?
records.proposed_answer: Under Section 61 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (in force since 1 July 2024 under S.O. 849(E)), nothing in the Adhiniyam shall apply to deny the admissibility of an electronic or digital record in evidence solely on the ground that it is an electronic or digital record. Such record has the same legal effect, validity, and enforceability as other documents, but is expressly subject to Section 63. The Explanation incorporates the definition in clause (t) of Section 2(1) of the Information Technology Act, 2000, and the proviso mandates that any electronic record produced in evidence must be accompanied by a certificate under Section 63(4).

evidence_passages.verbatim_text: Nothing in this Adhiniyam shall apply to deny the admissibility of an electronic or digital record in the evidence on the ground that it is an electronic or digital record, and such record shall have the same legal effect, validity and enforceability as other document, subject to the provisions of section 63.

For the purposes of this section, an electronic or digital record includes records stored, generated, received or sent in an electronic form or micro-films, computer-generated fiche and any other form as defined in clause (t) of sub-section (1) of section 2 of the Information Technology Act, 2000.
(t) "electronic record" means data, record or data generated, image or sound stored, received or sent in an electronic form or micro film or computer generated micro fiche;

records.question: Under Section 63 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, when is electronic information deemed to be a document and who must sign the accompanying certificate?
records.proposed_answer: Under Section 63(1) of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (in force since 1 July 2024 under S.O. 849(E)), any information contained in an electronic record which is printed on paper, stored, recorded, or copied in optical or magnetic media shall be deemed to be also a document. Under Section 63(2), the computer output must be produced during a period of regular use with regular input of information, provided that the certificate signed by a person in official charge shall be produced in evidence.

records.question: Can an electronic record be admitted in evidence under Section 61 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 without complying with Section 63?
records.proposed_answer: No. Section 61 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (in force since 1 July 2024 under S.O. 849(E)) explicitly states that the legal effect, validity, and enforceability of an electronic or digital record is 'subject to the provisions of section 63'. Furthermore, the proviso to Section 61 specifies that where any electronic record is produced in evidence, it shall be accompanied by a certificate referred to in sub-section (4) of Section 63.

records.question: What elements constitute a computer related offence under Section 66 of the Information Technology Act, 2000 and what punishment is prescribed?
records.proposed_answer: Under Section 66 of the Information Technology Act, 2000 (in force w.e.f. 27 October 2009 pursuant to Act 10 of 2009), if any person, dishonestly or fraudulently, does any act referred to in Section 43, he commits a computer related offence and shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years or with fine which may extend to five lakh rupees or with both. The Explanation clarifies that 'dishonestly' and 'fraudulently' carry the meanings assigned to them in Section 24 and Section 25 of the Indian Penal Code.

evidence_passages.verbatim_text:
1 [66. Computer related offences.-If any person, dishonestly or fraudulently, does any act referred to in section 43, he shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years or with fine which may extend to five lakh rupees or with both.

Explanation.-For the purposes of this section,-

(a) the word "dishonestly" shall have the meaning assigned to it in section 24 of the Indian Penal Code (45 of 1860);

(b) the word "fraudulently" shall have the meaning assigned to it in section 25 of the Indian Penal Code (45 of 1860).

records.question: What ingredients constitute the offence of identity theft under Section 66C of the Information Technology Act, 2000 and what is the penalty?
records.proposed_answer: Under Section 66C of the Information Technology Act, 2000 (in force w.e.f. 27 October 2009 under Act 10 of 2009), whoever fraudulently or dishonestly makes use of the electronic signature, password, or any other unique identification feature of any other person commits identity theft. records.question: Which judicial forums possess jurisdiction to grant anticipatory bail under Section 482(1) of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023?
records.proposed_answer: Under Section 482(1) of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (in force since 1 July 2024 under Notification S.O. 848(E)), when any person has reason to believe that he may be arrested on an accusation of having committed a non-bailable offence, he may apply to either the High Court or the Court of Session for a direction under Section 482, and that Court may, if it thinks fit, direct that in the event of such arrest, he shall be released on bail.

records.question: How are criminal appeals, applications, trials, and investigations pending immediately before 1 July 2024 governed under Section 531(2)(a) of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023?
records.proposed_answer: Under Section 531(1) of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (in force since 1 July 2024 under S.O. 848(E)), the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 is repealed. However, under Section 531(2)(a), if immediately before 1 July 2024 there was any appeal, application, trial, inquiry, or investigation pending, such proceeding shall be disposed of, continued, held, or made in accordance with the provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 as if the BNSS had not come into force.
